proposal.title: Moby Dick; or The Whale
proposal.gist: A castaway sailor joins Captain Ahab's obsessive, fatal hunt for the white whale Moby Dick, which destroys ship and crew.
proposal.question: Moby Dick — can one man's vengeance against an indifferent universe end in anything but ruin? (a voyage ending in catastrophe)

children.title: Loomings
children.gist: Ishmael, restless and drawn to the sea, resolves to ship out as a common sailor on a whaling voyage, sensing fate steering him toward one particular ship.
children.question: Ishmael's going to sea — why does a landsman feel compelled toward whaling and toward this voyage specifically? (a first-person reflection)

children.title: Title and credits
children.gist: The title page identifies Moby Dick by Herman Melville and gives basic publication framing.

children.title: Table of contents
children.gist: A full chapter listing for the novel, from Loomings to the Epilogue.

children.title: Transcriber's notes
children.gist: A note explaining this etext combines earlier Project Gutenberg and Virginia Tech versions, checked against a print copy.

children.title: Why Ishmael goes to sea
children.gist: Ishmael explains that whenever he grows depressed on land he escapes to sea, always as a common sailor rather than passenger or officer, for pay, fresh air, and relief from melancholy.

children.title: Fate steers him to whaling
children.gist: Ishmael reflects that some unaccountable providence, not mere choice, pushed him specifically toward a whaling voyage, drawn by curiosity about the great whale and distant, perilous seas.

children.title: The Spouter-Inn and Queequeg
children.gist: In New Bedford, Ishmael unexpectedly beds down with the tattooed harpooneer Queequeg, and the two form an unlikely, deep friendship before signing aboard together.
children.question: Queequeg the cannibal harpooneer — can true fellowship form across savage and Christian, stranger and stranger? (a bedfellow story)

children.title: The Carpet-Bag
children.gist: Ishmael arrives alone in New Bedford on a freezing December night with little money, wanders past costlier inns, and settles on the shabby Spouter-Inn for cheap lodging.

children.title: The Spouter-Inn
children.gist: Inside the eerie, whale-themed Spouter-Inn Ishmael learns he must share a bed with an unseen harpooneer, panics on meeting the tattooed, head-peddling Queequeg at night, but after mutual fright the two calmly agree to share the bed as strangers turned bedfellows.

children.title: The Counterpane
children.gist: Waking tangled in Queequeg's tattooed arm recalls a childhood memory of an unexplained supernatural hand, and Ishmael watches with curious affection as Queequeg dresses in his own odd, half-civilized way.

children.title: Breakfast
children.gist: At breakfast among a company of oddly bashful, weather-tanned whalemen, Queequeg sits coolly at the head of the table using his harpoon to spear steaks, untroubled by ordinary table manners.

children.title: The Street
children.gist: Strolling New Bedford's streets, Ishmael marvels at cannibal harpooneers mixing with green farm boys turned whalemen, and credits the town's grand houses and gardens entirely to fortunes harpooned from the sea.

children.title: The Chapel
children.gist: Visiting the Whaleman's Chapel before sailing, Ishmael reads memorial tablets to drowned sailors with no graves, and concludes from their quiet grief that his true self is not his perishable body, so no stove boat can truly destroy him.

children.title: The Pulpit
children.gist: Father Mapple, a former sailor turned beloved preacher, climbs a rope ladder into a ship-bow-shaped pulpit and then draws the ladder up after him, symbolizing his withdrawal into pure communion with God.

children.title: The Sermon
children.gist: Father Mapple preaches the story of Jonah as a double lesson, warning that disobeying God's hard commands brings punishment, while a preacher who flees duty to please rather than appall men is cast away, yet true delight comes from defying worldly power for God's truth.

children.title: A Bosom Friend
children.gist: Returning from chapel, Ishmael watches Queequeg whittle his idol and count pages, then grows fond of his calm self-sufficiency, shares a pipe and money with him, and reasons by the golden rule that joining Queequeg's idol worship is itself true worship of God.

children.title: Nightgown
children.gist: Lying wakeful together in the cold inn, Ishmael muses that true warmth is felt only by contrast with cold, and persuades Queequeg, now sharing his pipe freely, to recount the story of his life.

children.title: Biographical
children.gist: Born a king's son on the island of Rokovoko, Queequeg forced his way aboard a visiting ship to see Christendom, found Christian sailors no better than his own people, and resolves to sail with Ishmael to Nantucket as a working harpooneer.

children.title: Wheelbarrow
children.gist: Wheeling their luggage to the Nantucket packet, Queequeg tells comic stories of his own cultural misunderstandings, then on the voyage calmly humiliates a mocking passenger before heroically diving overboard to rescue him from drowning.

children.title: Nantucket
children.gist: Nantucket is portrayed as a barren sandy outpost whose settlers, born on its beach, grew from catching crabs to commanding a worldwide whaling empire, so that in effect two thirds of the sea's business belongs to them.

children.title: Chowder
children.gist: At the fish-obsessed Try Pots inn run by the scolding Mrs. Hussey, Ishmael and Queequeg are served delicious clam and cod chowders in turn, and the harpoon is confiscated for the night after a past boarder's fatal accident.

children.title: The Ship
children.gist: Guided by Queequeg's idol Yojo, Ishmael chooses the strange, trophy-decked Pequod and negotiates a modest share of profits from its gruff owners Peleg and quibbling Bildad, who first mention the mysterious, one-legged Captain Ahab who lost his leg to a whale.

children.title: The Ramadan
children.gist: Alarmed when Queequeg's door stays locked all day during his Ramadan fast, Ishmael eventually breaks in to find him silently squatting with his idol, and later argues gently that such extreme religious self-denial is needless and unhealthy.

children.title: His Mark
children.gist: When Peleg and Bildad balk at taking aboard a cannibal, Ishmael talks his way past their religious objections, Queequeg proves his skill by spearing a tar-spot with his harpoon, and he signs the ship's articles with his tattooed mark for a ninetieth lay.

children.title: The Prophet
children.gist: A shabby, pockmarked stranger named Elijah accosts Ishmael and Queequeg with cryptic warnings about Captain Ahab's past misfortunes and their fate aboard the Pequod, leaving Ishmael unsettled but ultimately dismissing him as a humbug.

children.title: All Astir
children.gist: As the Pequod is provisioned for its three-year voyage by Bildad, Peleg, and the tirelessly kind Aunt Charity, Ishmael grows uneasy that Captain Ahab remains unseen, though he suppresses his doubts rather than confront them.

children.title: Going Aboard
children.gist: Boarding the Pequod before dawn, Ishmael and Queequeg are again accosted by the ominous Elijah asking about mysterious men boarding the ship, then discover from a sleepy rigger that Captain Ahab secretly came aboard the previous night.

children.title: Merry Christmas
children.gist: On a cold Christmas morning the Pequod sets sail under Peleg's rough commands and Bildad's pious hymns, and the two old owners reluctantly bid an emotional, fussily detailed farewell before rowing back to shore.

children.title: The Lee Shore
children.gist: Ishmael singles out the sailor Bulkington at the helm and meditates that true, fearless thought must resist the false safety of the shore, embracing the perilous open sea as the only place of real independence and truth.

children.title: The Advocate
children.gist: Ishmael defends whaling's reputation by cataloguing its economic scale, its pioneering role opening Australia, Japan, and South American trade, and its literary and royal associations, insisting the profession deserves far more honor than it receives.

children.title: Postscript
children.gist: As a final jab in whaling's defense, Ishmael notes that the sacred oil used to anoint kings and queens at their coronations is, in fact, nothing but unrefined sperm whale oil supplied by whalemen.

children.title: Knights and Squires: Starbuck
children.gist: Chief mate Starbuck is portrayed as a lean, steady Nantucket Quaker whose courage is practical rather than reckless, yet whose deep superstition and grief over lost kin leave him vulnerable to being overwhelmed by a truly terrifying man.

children.title: Knights and Squires: Stubb, Flask, Harpooneers
children.gist: Second mate Stubb faces danger with careless good humor fueled by constant pipe-smoking, third mate Flask treats whale-hunting as mere sport, and the ship's three harpooneers—Queequeg, the Native American Tashtego, and the giant African Daggoo—are paired as squires to each mate among a crew of isolated foreign-born sailors.

children.title: Ahab
children.gist: After days unseen, Captain Ahab finally appears on deck bearing a livid scar down his face and an ivory leg carved from whalebone, standing rigid in his pivot-hole with an expression of grim, unshakable, almost tragic fixed purpose.

children.title: Enter Ahab; to Him, Stubb
children.gist: A chapter heading introducing a coming scene between Ahab and Stubb.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 29. Enter Ahab; to Him, Stubb.

children.title: Ahab reveals his quest
children.gist: Ahab nails a gold doubloon to the mast and swears the crew to hunt Moby Dick, the white whale that maimed him, over Starbuck's moral objections, binding all hands to his private vengeance.
children.question: The quarter-deck oath — how does Ahab turn a crew's ordinary trade into a shared pact of vengeance against one whale? (a dramatic scene)

children.title: Ahab's growing obsession
children.gist: Tropical nights deepen Ahab's brooding, and when Stubb gently suggests muffling his ivory leg's noise, Ahab explodes with scorn, leaving Stubb bewildered and half-wondering if he should pray for the strange old captain.

children.title: The Pipe
children.gist: Seated like a sea-king on his ivory stool, Ahab finds his pipe no longer soothing his restless mind and, declaring it meant for calmer men, flings it still burning into the sea.

children.title: Queen Mab
children.gist: Stubb recounts to Flask a bizarre dream in which Ahab's ivory leg kicks him and a merman convinces him the kick was an honor rather than an insult, teaching him never to retaliate, just before Ahab himself shouts orders to watch for a white whale.

children.title: Cetology
children.gist: Before the chase truly begins, the narrator pauses to attempt a classification of whales, admitting that past naturalists like Scoresby, Beale, Cuvier and Hunter all confess the subject is confused and nearly impossible to systematize.

children.title: Cetology and whaling craft
children.gist: The narrative pauses over many chapters to classify whales, detail the mechanics and dangers of the hunt, and anatomize the sperm whale's body, grounding the chase in exhaustive natural and nautical knowledge.
children.question: The whale explained — what encyclopedic account of the creature and its hunting does the book offer between dramatic turns? (a long technical survey)

children.title: Cetology classification
children.gist: Ishmael devises a rough classification of all whale species by size—Folio, Octavo, Duodecimo—since neither baleen, hump, nor anatomy allows a cleaner system, and declares the project permanently unfinished.

children.title: The Specksnyder
children.gist: Explains that the old Dutch whaling office of Specksnyder once split command between captain and chief harpooneer, and shows Ahab, though demanding instant obedience, still observing the sea's customary forms for his own private ends.

children.title: The Cabin-Table
children.gist: Describes the strict, almost sacred etiquette of meals in Ahab's cabin, where mates eat in silent deference before him and the three harpooneers later feast with boisterous freedom after their masters leave.

children.title: The Mast-Head
children.gist: Ishmael recounts the history and discomfort of standing mast-head watch, then confesses that his own dreamy, philosophical reveries aloft made him a careless lookout, warning ship-owners against hiring such meditative young men.

children.title: The Quarter-Deck
children.gist: Ahab nails a gold doubloon to the mast, reveals that Moby Dick took his leg, and compels the crew—over Starbuck's moral protest—to swear a drunken oath to hunt the white whale to its death.

children.title: Sunset
children.gist: Alone in his cabin at sunset, Ahab confesses that beauty no longer touches him, embraces his own madness as fixed purpose, and vows that nothing—fate, gods, or men—can swerve him from his course.

children.title: Dusk
children.gist: Starbuck, leaning against the mainmast, laments that his sane will is overmastered by Ahab's madness yet feels bound to help him anyway, finding only thin hope in the whale's vast ocean to roam.

children.title: First Night-Watch
children.gist: Stubb, mending a rope at the foretop, laughs off his unease about Ahab's quest by deciding everything is predestined, resolving to meet whatever comes with jokes and song rather than dread.

children.title: Midnight, Forecastle
children.gist: The crew of many nations sing, dance, and quarrel on the forecastle at midnight until a squall interrupts them, leaving the small black cabin boy Pip terrified by their oath to hunt Moby Dick.

children.title: Moby Dick
children.gist: Ishmael explains how rumor, superstition, and real documented ferocity built Moby Dick's terrifying reputation among whalemen, and traces how Ahab's leg-wound curdled into a monomania that identifies all evil with the one whale.

children.title: The Whiteness of the Whale
children.gist: Ishmael meditates on why whiteness, though linked to purity and holiness in many traditions, becomes uniquely terrifying when joined to something fearsome, and suggests the color's blankness mirrors the universe's own dread meaninglessness.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 42. The Whiteness of the Whale.

children.title: Hark!
children.gist: Two sailors on night watch argue over a strange cough-like noise from the after-hold, hinting that someone unknown is hidden aboard the Pequod, a mystery the Mogul captain seems already to know about.

children.title: The Chart
children.gist: Ahab pores nightly over sea-charts and whaling logs, using known currents and seasonal whale migrations to calculate the one time and place—the Season-on-the-Line—where he is most likely to finally meet Moby Dick.

children.title: The Affidavit
children.gist: Ishmael marshals real-world testimony—repeated strikes on the same whale, famous named whales, and ships like the Essex sunk by deliberate ramming—to prove that Moby Dick's ferocity is no exaggerated fable but plain fact.

children.title: Surmises
children.gist: Ahab calculates that he must still pursue ordinary whaling and pay, since his crew's chase of Moby Dick alone cannot sustain their loyalty, and he must avoid the charge of usurping the ship's purpose.

children.title: The Mat-Maker
children.gist: While weaving a mat with Queequeg, Ishmael muses that necessity, free will, and chance interweave like the loom's threads, until Tashtego's wild cry from the masthead announces the first whale sighting of the voyage.

children.title: The First Lowering
children.gist: The crew lowers boats to chase whales and Ahab's own secret boat crew—the turbaned Fedallah and four Manila men stowed aboard—is revealed, before a sudden squall capsizes Starbuck's boat and nearly drowns its men.

children.title: The Hyena
children.gist: Shaken by the squall, Ishmael adopts a grim, joking philosophy toward life's perils, learns such capsizings are routine in whaling, and goes below to draw up his will with Queequeg as witness.

children.title: Ahab's Boat and Crew. Fedallah
children.gist: Explains how Ahab secretly prepared his own boat and recruited the mysterious Fedallah and his four companions as a private crew, whose origin and uncanny hold over Ahab remain wholly unexplained.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 50. Ahab's Boat and Crew. Fedallah.

children.title: The Spirit-Spout
children.gist: A silvery, moonlit spout, first spotted by Fedallah, lures the Pequod onward for nights before vanishing each time, feeding superstitious dread among the crew as the ship rounds the stormy Cape of Good Hope.

children.title: The Albatross
children.gist: The Pequod hails a weathered, four-year whaler called the Goney to ask after Moby Dick, but wind prevents a proper exchange, and Ahab, sensing the fish fleeing his wake, orders the ship onward round the world.

children.title: The Gam
children.gist: Ishmael explains the whaling custom of the 'gam'—a social visit between crews of meeting whale-ships—and notes the peculiar etiquette by which a gamming captain must stand stiffly in his boat without support.

children.title: The Town-Ho's Story
children.gist: Ishmael retells, for a circle of Spanish listeners in Lima, the Town-Ho's secret story of the sailor Steelkilt's mutiny against a brutal mate and how Moby Dick himself finally delivered the fatal revenge.

children.title: Monstrous Pictures of Whales
children.gist: Ishmael surveys centuries of paintings and sculptures of whales, from Hindu temple carvings to Dutch engravings, arguing that every one of them wildly misrepresents the living creature's true form.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 55. Of the Monstrous Pictures of Whales.

children.title: Less Erroneous Whale Pictures
children.gist: Comparing the handful of known whale illustrators, Ishmael judges the French painter Garnery's dramatic engravings of whale hunts the truest and most vivid, far surpassing dry English and American outlines.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 56. Of the Less Erroneous Pictures of Whales, and the True Pictures of Whaling Scenes.

children.title: Whales in Folk Art
children.gist: Whale images appear everywhere beyond formal art, on beggars' signboards, carved into teeth and wood by sailors, as weathercocks, and even imagined in cliffs, mountains, and constellations.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 57. Of Whales in Paint; in Teeth; in Wood; in Sheet-Iron; in Stone; in Mountains; in Stars.

children.title: Brit
children.gist: Sailing through vast golden meadows of brit that Right Whales feed on, Ishmael turns from this strange beauty to brood on the sea's universal, indifferent cruelty toward all living things.

children.title: Squid
children.gist: A ghostly giant squid, rarely glimpsed by any whaling crew, rises beside the Pequod and is briefly mistaken for Moby Dick, leaving Starbuck shaken by its formless, unearthly appearance.

children.title: The Line
children.gist: Ishmael details the whale-line's material, coiling, and placement throughout the boat, stressing how its hidden, snakelike danger can snatch an oarsman to his death in an instant.

children.title: Stubb Kills a Whale
children.gist: Roused from a drowsy mast-head trance, the crew spots a sperm whale, and Stubb, smoking his pipe through the whole chase, lances and kills it after a wild, dangerous pursuit.

children.title: The Dart
children.gist: Ishmael argues that exhausting the harpooneer with rowing before he must throw his weapon causes most failed strikes, and that the headsman should instead stay fresh in the bow throughout the chase.

children.title: The Crotch
children.gist: The crotch, a notched stick holding two harpoons ready to hand, lets whalemen double their chances of a lasting strike, though the loose second iron becomes its own floating hazard.

children.title: Stubb's Supper
children.gist: While towing the dead whale through a night thronged with feeding sharks, Stubb feasts on whale steak and comically badgers old Fleece the cook into mock-preaching a sermon to the sharks.

children.title: The Whale as a Dish
children.gist: Ishmael surveys the odd history of eating whale meat, arguing that civilized squeamishness about devouring the creature is hypocritical given humanity's casual cruelty toward other animals.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 65. The Whale as a Dish.

children.title: The Shark Massacre
children.gist: Overnight, swarms of sharks gather to devour the moored carcass, and Queequeg and a shipmate spear them by lantern light, discovering the creatures' ferocious vitality even when disemboweled.

children.title: Cutting In
children.gist: Ishmael narrates the laborious nighttime ritual of cutting-in, in which tackles and spades strip the whale's blubber from its body in one continuous spiraling strip, like peeling an orange.

children.title: The Blanket
children.gist: Ishmael argues the thick blubber, not the thin outer film, is the whale's true skin, marvels at its mysterious engraved markings, and credits this blanket with keeping its blood warm in Arctic seas.

children.title: The Funeral
children.gist: The stripped, headless carcass is cut loose and drifts away, attracting sharks and screaming birds in a mocking funeral, and its floating remains later mislead sailors into charting false reefs.

children.title: The Sphynx
children.gist: Alone beside the suspended, decapitated sperm whale's head, Ahab broods aloud, begging the silent head to reveal the drowned world's secrets it alone among all divers has witnessed.

children.title: The Jeroboam's Story
children.gist: The plague-stricken ship Jeroboam, ruled by a deranged self-proclaimed archangel named Gabriel, reports that Moby Dick has already killed one officer, and Gabriel violently refuses Ahab a dead man's letter.

children.title: The Monkey-Rope
children.gist: Tied to Queequeg by a rope that binds their fates together while Queequeg works atop the shark-infested carcass, Ishmael reflects that every person is likewise bound helplessly to others' fortunes.

children.title: Stubb and Flask Kill a Right Whale
children.gist: After killing an unwanted Right Whale for a superstition about balancing the ship, Stubb and Flask gossip uneasily about the sinister Parsee Fedallah, whom Stubb suspects is the devil bargaining for Ahab's soul.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 73. Stubb and Flask kill a Right Whale; and Then Have a Talk over Him.

children.title: Sperm Whale's Head
children.gist: Examining the sperm whale's suspended head, Ishmael details its dignified shape, oddly sideways-placed eyes giving it two separate fields of vision, tiny ears, cavernous jaw, and rows of teeth.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 74. The Sperm Whale's Head—Contrasted View.

children.title: Right Whale's Head
children.gist: Turning to the Right Whale's opposite head, Ishmael describes its sulky hanging lip, baleen blinds that strain food from water, and fleshy tongue, concluding the two whales' heads share almost nothing.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 75. The Right Whale's Head—Contrasted View.

children.title: The Battering-Ram
children.gist: Ishmael argues the sperm whale's blunt, boneless, nerveless forehead is an unimaginably tough battering ram, strong enough, he insists readers must accept, to have actually sunk a ship by ramming alone.

children.title: The Great Heidelburgh Tun
children.gist: The whale's forehead conceals the Case, a great reservoir likened to the famous Heidelburgh wine tun, holding hundreds of gallons of the purest, most prized spermaceti oil.

children.title: Cistern and Buckets
children.gist: While bailing spermaceti from the suspended head, Tashtego slips and falls into the case and nearly drowns, until Queequeg dives in and dramatically delivers him in a feat likened to midwifery.

children.title: The Prairie
children.gist: Ishmael attempts to read the sperm whale's vast, noseless, mouthless brow through physiognomy, concluding its blank, god-like forehead expresses an unfathomable, silent genius no science can decipher.

children.title: The Nut
children.gist: Turning to phrenology, Ishmael finds the sperm whale's actual brain surprisingly small and hidden, and proposes instead reading character in its massive spinal cord, crediting its hump to sheer indomitable will.

children.title: The Pequod Meets The Virgin
children.gist: The oil-starved German ship Jungfrau loses a frantic multi-boat race to an old crippled whale, which the Pequod's men kill, only for the corpse's strange sinking tendency to nearly capsize their own ship.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 81. The Pequod Meets The Virgin.

children.title: The Honor and Glory of Whaling
children.gist: Ishmael mock-seriously claims whaling's nobility by tracing a mythic lineage of whalemen through Perseus, St. George, Hercules, Jonah, and the god Vishnu, each supposedly linked to a whale.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 82. The Honor and Glory of Whaling.

children.title: Jonah Historically Regarded
children.gist: Ishmael mocks a skeptical old whaleman's objections to the Bible's Jonah story, rehearsing and ironically dismantling rationalizing theories meant to reconcile the miracle with geography and anatomy.

children.title: Pitchpoling
children.gist: Queequeg's superstitious greasing of the boat precedes Stubb's display of pitchpoling, a difficult technique of hurling the lance accurately from a racing boat to finish off a fleeing whale.

children.title: The Fountain
children.gist: Ishmael investigates whether the whale's spout is water or mist, explains the creature's single nostril and oxygen-storing blood vessels, and concludes, poetically, that the spout is likely just vapor.

children.title: The Tail
children.gist: Ishmael praises the sperm whale's tail as the seat of its strength, delicacy, and beauty, cataloguing its five distinct motions from propulsion and battle to the sublime upward peaking before a dive.

children.title: The Grand Armada
children.gist: A chapter heading only; its narrative content begins beyond this section's final block.

children.title: Encounters and omens at sea
children.gist: The Pequod gams with other whaling ships, hears escalating tales and warnings about Moby Dick's deadliness, loses crew to accident, and accumulates portents while Ahab's fixation visibly consumes him.
children.question: Ships met at sea — do the Pequod's encounters warn Ahab off his hunt, or only confirm his fatal course? (several ship meetings)

children.title: The Grand Armada
children.gist: Nearing the Straits of Sunda the Pequod is drawn into a vast herd of sperm whales, chased by Malay pirates, and plunges into the herd's calm inner lake where Queequeg's boat drifts among nursing whales before a wounded whale panics the mass and the hunt yields only one capture.

children.title: Schools and Schoolmasters
children.gist: Sperm whales travel in smaller schools led either by a harem-master bull guarding his females or by packs of pugnacious young bulls, and the oldest males eventually separate to live alone as solitary, so-called lone whales.

children.title: Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish
children.gist: Whalers settle ownership disputes by a simple code—a Fast-Fish belongs to whoever is attached to it, a Loose-Fish to whoever catches it first—and the narrator extends this doctrine satirically to property, empire, and all human claims of possession.

children.title: Heads or Tails
children.gist: Under an old English law the King gets a captured whale's head and the Queen its tail, and a true anecdote shows this right delegated to the Duke of Wellington, who kept poor fishermen's whole catch despite their hardship and pleas.

children.title: The Pequod Meets The Rose-Bud
children.gist: Stubb tricks a foolish French captain into abandoning two foul-smelling dead whales by inventing a story about disease, so he can secretly dig into one carcass and extract valuable ambergris for himself.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 91. The Pequod Meets The Rose-Bud.

children.title: Ambergris
children.gist: Ambergris, a fragrant waxy substance prized in perfumery and found only in sick sperm whales' bowels, proves that something precious can arise from decay, and the chapter defends whales generally against the charge of smelling foul.

children.title: The Castaway
children.gist: Timid Pip twice leaps from Stubb's whaleboat in panic, and the second time Stubb leaves him behind in the vast ocean, an abandonment that drives Pip mad but also grants him a strange, unearthly spiritual vision of the deep.

children.title: A Squeeze of the Hand
children.gist: Squeezing cooled lumps of spermaceti back into liquid with his crewmates fills the narrator with an overwhelming, almost mystical feeling of universal affection, prompting him to locate happiness not in ambition but in simple domestic comforts.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 94. A Squeeze of the Hand.

children.title: The Cassock
children.gist: The whale's long black genital organ is skinned, stretched, and worn by the mincer as a robe while he slices blubber into thin sheets for the try-pots, an irreverent image the narrator likens to a priest's vestments.

children.title: The Try-Works
children.gist: Standing a midnight watch at the ship's fiery brick try-works, the narrator nearly capsizes the Pequod after dozing and losing his bearings, drawing from this a warning against staring too long into fire or despair rather than facing life's truth directly.

children.title: The Lamp
children.gist: Unlike ordinary sailors who live in darkness, whalemen burn abundant pure oil in their berths so that even belowdecks the ship glows with light, a small luxury unique to their trade.

children.title: Stowing Down and Clearing Up
children.gist: After the oil is cooled, casked, and stowed below, the filthy ship and crew are scrubbed spotless within a day or two, only for the cry of a new whale sighting to plunge them back into bloody, exhausting labor all over again.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 98. Stowing Down and Clearing Up.

children.title: The Doubloon
children.gist: A gold coin nailed to the mast as a reward becomes a mirror for the crew's characters, as Ahab, Starbuck, Stubb, Flask, the Manxman, Queequeg, Fedallah, and the half-mad Pip each read into its zodiac symbols their own obsessions, fears, or despair.

children.title: Leg and Arm
children.gist: Meeting the English whaler Samuel Enderby, Ahab learns from its one-armed captain Boomer, who lost his arm to Moby Dick and now wisely avoids him, a story that only inflames Ahab's own reckless determination to hunt the whale regardless of the cost.

children.title: The Decanter
children.gist: The narrator praises the historic Enderby whaling firm's pioneering voyages and recalls a lavish, drunken gam aboard the Samuel Enderby, tracing English whalers' famous hospitality back to old Dutch provisioning customs recorded in a quaint translated ledger.

children.title: A Bower in the Arsacides
children.gist: The narrator explains that his unique knowledge of a full-grown sperm whale's skeleton comes from measuring one enshrined as a sacred relic in a jungle temple on the island of Tranque, where vines and priests had made it an object of worship.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 102. A Bower in the Arsacides.

children.title: Measurement of The Whale's Skeleton
children.gist: Detailed measurements of the Tranque skeleton's skull, vertebrae, and ribs reveal that bare bones vastly understate the whale's living bulk, since flesh and blubber once filled out dimensions the skeleton alone cannot show.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 103. Measurement of The Whale's Skeleton.

children.title: The Fossil Whale
children.gist: Fossil whale bones found across Europe, America, and ancient Egyptian temples prove the whale's lineage predates humanity itself, making Leviathan an almost timeless creature whose ancestry reaches back before recorded history began.

children.title: Does the Whale's Magnitude Diminish?
children.gist: Comparing fossil and modern whales, and whale hunting to the swift extermination of American buffalo, the narrator argues whales have not shrunk and, thanks to their vast ocean refuge and long lifespans, cannot be hunted to extinction like land animals.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 105. Does the Whale's Magnitude Diminish?—Will He Perish?

children.title: Ahab's leg and final signs
children.gist: Ahab gets a new ivory leg forged, breaks his quadrant, reverses his compass in a typhoon, and loses his life-buoy and mast-head lookout, each mishap read as a fated sign before the final confrontation.
children.question: Ahab's mounting omens — why do broken instruments and lost men fail to turn Ahab from his course? (a chain of bad signs)

children.title: Ahab's Leg
children.gist: Ahab's ivory leg cracks again after a violent exit from another ship, recalling an earlier near-fatal accident, so he orders the carpenter to forge him a sturdier replacement overnight.

children.title: The Carpenter
children.gist: The ship's carpenter is portrayed as a tireless, oddly impersonal jack-of-all-trades who fixes anything mechanical without reflection, his strange vitality making him seem almost a machine with a soul.

children.title: Ahab and the Carpenter
children.gist: Watching his new leg being filed, Ahab needles the carpenter with riddles about phantom pain and lost limbs, musing darkly that a soul might suffer bodilessly forever, as the man builds him a bone.

children.title: Ahab and Starbuck in the Cabin
children.gist: When Starbuck reports a leaking oil cask and urges Ahab to stop and fix it, Ahab furiously refuses and nearly threatens him with a musket, only relenting at the last moment to order the hold opened.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 109. Ahab and Starbuck in the Cabin.

children.title: Queequeg in His Coffin
children.gist: Dying of fever, Queequeg has the carpenter build him a canoe-shaped coffin to his own specifications, tests it while alive, then suddenly decides to live because of unfinished business, and later carves its lid with his tattoos' mysteries.

children.title: The Pacific
children.gist: Entering the vast, dreamlike Pacific Ocean fills Ishmael with reverent wonder at its hidden mystery, while Ahab, unmoved by such poetry, feels only his purpose sharpen as he nears the Japanese grounds where Moby Dick swims.

children.title: The Blacksmith
children.gist: Perth the blacksmith, ruined by drink and loss of home, family, and livelihood ashore, found in whaling a refuge from grief, his patient hammering at the forge embodying a man who has given up on life but keeps working anyway.

children.title: The Forge
children.gist: Ahab brings Perth old horseshoe nails and commands him to forge a special harpoon, which he welds himself, tempers in the harpooneers' blood rather than water, and baptizes in Satan's name, dedicating it entirely to killing Moby Dick.

children.title: The Gilder
children.gist: Calm, golden seas briefly lull the crew into dreamy peace, with Starbuck and Stubb voicing contrasting hopeful moods, while Ahab reflects that life's gentlest moments never last and leave him unchanged in his grim purpose.

children.title: The Pequod Meets The Bachelor
children.gist: A jubilant, fully-loaded Nantucket ship bound home with no interest in Moby Dick sails past the grim Pequod, and Ahab, refusing its captain's cheerful invitation aboard, presses on in stark contrast to its celebration.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 115. The Pequod Meets The Bachelor.

children.title: The Dying Whale
children.gist: After a successful hunt, Ahab watches a dying sperm whale turn its head toward the setting sun in its final moments, and reads into this strange ritual a dark, fatalistic philosophy about life, death, and an indifferent sea.

children.title: The Whale Watch
children.gist: Keeping watch overnight beside a slain whale, Ahab and the Parsee Fedallah exchange a cryptic prophecy about two hearses, strangling rope, and Fedallah dying first as his pilot, which Ahab takes as proof of his own immortality.

children.title: The Quadrant
children.gist: Furious that his quadrant can fix his position but not locate Moby Dick, Ahab curses science and smashes the instrument to the deck, declaring he will instead navigate by compass and dead reckoning alone.

children.title: The Candles
children.gist: During a violent typhoon, the masts blaze with eerie corpusant fire; Ahab seizes the burning links, defiantly worships the flame as his fiery father, and blows it out to cow the terrified crew back into following his vow against the White Whale.

children.title: The Deck Towards the End of the First Night Watch
children.gist: As the storm rages, Starbuck asks permission to shorten sail and secure the anchors, but Ahab refuses to strike anything, insisting the wind has not yet reached dangerous strength for him.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 120. The Deck Towards the End of the First Night Watch.

children.title: Midnight.—The Forecastle Bulwarks
children.gist: Lashing down the anchors in the storm, Stubb argues to Flask that lightning rods and prior warnings about doom were overblown fears, insisting ordinary sailors face no more danger than anyone else at sea.

children.title: Midnight Aloft.—Thunder and Lightning
children.gist: High on the main-top-sail yard amid the storm, Tashtego grumbles that thunder is useless and wishes instead for rum, a brief comic complaint against the tempest's noise.

children.title: The Musket
children.gist: Alone with a loaded musket outside Ahab's door, Starbuck agonizes over whether killing his captain would save the crew from doom, but ultimately cannot bring himself to do it and instead sends Stubb to wake Ahab.

children.title: The Needle
children.gist: The storm's lightning has reversed the ship's compass needles, but Ahab, undeterred, theatrically remagnetizes a sail-needle before the awestruck crew to restore their faith in his mastery, while privately comforting the traumatized boy Pip.

children.title: The Log and Line
children.gist: Ahab orders the rotted log-line heaved to measure the ship's speed, but it snaps and is lost, prompting his grim vow that he alone can mend all instruments, while Pip's ravings about his own abandonment unsettle everyone present.

children.title: The Life-Buoy
children.gist: After a sailor drowns because the ship's life-buoy has rotted and sunk with him, the crew lacks a replacement, so Queequeg suggests using his unused coffin, which Starbuck reluctantly orders converted despite its grim symbolism.

children.title: The Deck
children.gist: Ahab mocks the carpenter for simultaneously making legs, coffins, and now a life-buoy out of a coffin, musing uneasily that the symbol of death has become the ship's hope of survival, before retreating below with Pip.

children.title: The Pequod Meets The Rachel
children.gist: The grieving Captain Gardiner of the Rachel begs Ahab to help search for his missing son's whale-boat crew, including his twelve-year-old, but Ahab coldly refuses, unwilling to lose even hours in his pursuit of Moby Dick.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 128. The Pequod Meets The Rachel.

children.title: The Cabin
children.gist: Ahab tenderly but firmly forbids the devoted boy Pip from following him on the hunt, installing him instead in his own cabin chair, leaving Pip alone to ramble deliriously about his own abandonment and missing identity.

children.title: The Hat
children.gist: As Ahab's fixed purpose silences all levity aboard and he stands perpetual watch unsleeping beside the brooding Fedallah, he insists on being hoisted aloft himself to spot the whale first, only to have a hawk suddenly snatch his hat away as an ill omen.

children.title: The Pequod Meets The Delight
children.gist: A battered ship called, ironically, the Delight reveals a wrecked whale-boat and a dead crewman about to be buried at sea, having lost five men to Moby Dick, yet Ahab only brandishes his own harpoon and presses on past the burial.
children.sourceHeading: CHAPTER 131. The Pequod Meets The Delight.

children.title: The Symphony
children.gist: On a serene day blending gentle sky and powerful sea, Ahab weeps before Starbuck, confessing forty years of lonely, joyless whaling and longing for his wife and child, yet when Starbuck begs him to turn the ship home, Ahab, questioning what unseen force compels him, cannot break free of his fated chase.

children.title: The three-day chase
children.gist: Over three days Ahab pursues and finally attacks Moby Dick, who destroys the boats and then rams and sinks the Pequod itself, killing the crew and Ahab with his harpoon line.
children.question: The final chase — does Ahab's three-day hunt end in the whale's death or his own, and at what cost to all aboard? (a climactic three-day battle)

children.title: The Chase—First Day
children.gist: Ahab sights Moby Dick, lowers the boats, and the whale bites Ahab's boat in two, flinging him into the sea before the Pequod rescues the crew, leaving Ahab broken but unbowed and vowing to the doubloon's promise of gold.

children.title: The Chase—Second Day
children.gist: Moby Dick breaches and attacks all three boats at once, tangling their lines and smashing two together, snapping off Ahab's ivory leg and drowning Fedallah the Parsee, yet Ahab vows to hunt a third day despite Starbuck's pleas to stop.

children.title: The Chase—Third Day
children.gist: On the third day Ahab finds Moby Dick towing the Parsee's corpse lashed to his back, harpoons him again, and the enraged whale rams and sinks the Pequod itself, dragging Ahab down by his own harpoon line as the ship and crew vanish into the sea.

children.title: Epilogue heading
children.gist: This single heading marks the start of the book's closing section, with no further text given here.

children.title: Epilogue
children.gist: Ishmael alone survives the sinking, kept afloat by Queequeg's coffin-turned-life-buoy until the ship Rachel rescues him.
children.question: The sole survivor — how does Ishmael alone escape the wreck to tell this tale? (a brief closing account)
